title: Miami Winners and Losers: Roy's Redemption, Audi's Shadow, and the Stand-In's Farewell
meta: Published: 10 May 2026 | By Lena Müller, Strategy Analyst | F1CC News
caption: Jason Roy celebrates his first victory of 2026 – but the paddock’s attention is already on the stewards.
body:
Let’s rewind to lap 32, turn 8. Wesley Vandesteene has just lost the rear of his Mercedes and slammed into the wall. The safety car is deployed. Every team on the grid faces an instant decision: pit now for fresh tyres and sacrifice track position, or stay out and gamble on the race coming to them. Red Bull, with Jason Roy running in the fringes of the top five, choose the pit lane. They fit soft tyres. Roy emerges in second place. He takes the lead on lap 47 and never looks back. That single stop, executed under pressure, turned a midfield recovery drive into a grand prix victory. But while Roy celebrated, the shadow of a stewards’ investigation hung over the podium, and the radio waves carried the exhaustion of a grid pushed to its limit.

Winners

Jason Roy (Red Bull, P1 from P12): Roy’s victory was built on the pit wall’s decisiveness. The safety car erased his deficit and the soft tyres gave him the grip to hunt down Richard Hicks’ Audi. His overtake on Hicks around the outside of Turn 1 was the move of the race – brave, clean, and decisive. For a driver who had asked “why are we still here” as his car burned in Jeddah, this was redemption. He now sits on 54 points, and Red Bull are finally showing the pace that was promised.

Zhao Lei (McLaren, P2 from P8): Lei didn’t put a wheel wrong. He stayed out of trouble through the chaos, managed his tyres beautifully, and applied relentless pressure on the leaders in the closing laps. His second place, combined with Nathanial’s points finish, lifts McLaren to second in the constructors’ championship – and Lei to third in the drivers’ standings. The understated Chinese driver is now a genuine title contender.

Eren Aygen (Williams, P3 from pole): Pole position didn’t translate into a win, but Aygen’s third place was a study in resilience. He lost the lead to Hicks, then fought off both Audis in the final sprint to hold the podium. His championship challenge remains alive, and Williams are still in the constructors’ fight.

The medium‑tyre gamblers (Roy, Verhaeren, Swansson): The drivers who committed to medium tyres early in the race and used the safety car to switch to softs gained the most. Roy’s win, Verhaeren’s point, and Swansson’s solid midfield run were all built on the same strategic offset. The alternative – staying on a single compound through the caution – left drivers like Joshua Nathanial stranded on worn rubber, bleeding positions at the restart.

Losers

Audi (Hicks P4, Keisner P5 – provisional): Both Audis are under investigation. The results are provisional. Until the stewards rule, the paddock cannot fully celebrate their double points finish, nor can it write them off. The investigation, which began after qualifying, hangs over the team like a Florida thunderstorm. Hicks drove brilliantly to lead laps and fight for the podium; Keisner recovered from a poor qualifying to finish fifth. But if the penalty comes, all of that could be erased.

Wesley Vandesteene (Mercedes, DNF): His crash on lap 32 was the trigger for the safety car that reshaped the race. Vandesteene had been running in the points, but his season continues to oscillate between promise and disaster. The Mercedes is still not where the team wants it, and Vandesteene’s frustration is mounting.

Jack TEF (Williams, DNF): The stand‑in’s farewell ended in the wall. TEF’s radio message – “God damn guys… DNF. Sorry. Koop you mind taking one more race out so I can finish on a high?” – was met with a flat “Uhhhh no” from the recovering Lucas Koopman. TEF’s four‑race stint delivered a podium, a fourth place, and a mountain of goodwill. But he will hand the car back to Koopman in Canada with a wrecked machine and an unfulfilled wish for one more clean finish.

Sarah Springfield (Aston Martin, P16 after DSQs, 0 pts): “P18 and last of all cars running,” she tweeted. The promotion from the Audi disqualifications moves her to P16, but the points column remains blank. Aston Martin’s early‑season spark has dimmed, and Springfield’s frustration is no longer a secret.

Maikel Zwart (Mercedes, P10): A single point. A finish, at least, after Jeddah’s scream. But Zwart’s silence after the race was louder than any radio message. Mercedes are still searching for answers, and the upgraded engine hasn’t delivered the leap they needed. The Miami point is a crumb when the team needs a feast.

The drivers who missed the safety‑car window (Nathanial, Konstantaras, Wright): Joshua Nathanial stayed out on worn hards during the caution, believing the tyre life would hold. It didn’t. He dropped from the top five to ninth, losing points he couldn’t afford to lose. George Konstantaras and Lukas Wright were similarly stranded, their races undone not by pace but by timing.

Miami delivered a race of shifting fortunes, and the 2026 season continues to defy prediction. Roy is back. Audi are waiting. TEF is heading back to the pit wall. And the championship is tighter than ever. The circus heads to Canada with questions still unanswered – and a stewards’ verdict that could yet reshape the entire standings.
